newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac said "shocked" by Renault methods.
newsitem.headline: Chirac said "shocked" by Renault methods.

text.p: The French government intervened on Wednesday in a mounting furore over car maker Renault SA's decision to shut its Belgian factory, axing 3,100 jobs.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe summoned the recently privatised company's chairman to explain himself and President Jacques Chirac said he was shocked by the method used by Renault.

The statements reflected an abrupt change in tactics by the French authorities, who had previously avoided criticism of the firm's decision, announced last Thursday, to close its plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels.
They appeared to reflect concern at the damage to France's image and interests in Belgium and beyond, and at the risk of industrial unrest spreading to France.
Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted Chirac as telling the weekly cabinet meeting he was "shocked by the method" used by Renault, still 46-percent-owned by the French state.

Juppe told reporters: "The method was not right." He said he had summoned Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer for 1630 GMT on Wednesday "to tell him what I think" about the way Renault announced the Vilvoorde closure.

The company has since told staff it plans to cut a further 2,764 jobs in France this year, but without plant closures at its home base. Renault, privatised in two stages in 1994 and 1996, has 138,000 employees.
"The human dimension must not be neglected," Lamassoure quoted Juppe as telling the cabinet.

Several hundred Belgian Renault employees, facing redundancy in June, drove to France on Wednesday aboard 20 buses to picket a Renault factory at Douai, south of Lille. French trade unions declared solidarity with their Belgian comrades.
In Vilvoorde, home town of Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, sirens sounded and citizens observed five minutes' silence in protest while a black flag hung from the town hall.
Trade unions have called a one-hour work stoppage at Renault factories across Europe on Friday.

Lamassoure quoted Juppe as saying the Vilvoorde decision had caused "general and legitimate distress in Belgium as well as in France" and calling for "consultations to seek alternative solutions" respecting European, Belgian and French laws.
French media questioned the sudden indignation of the French authorities, saying it had been well aware of Renault's plans.

In a radio interview, Industry Minister Franck Borotra acknowledged that Renault had informed the French and Belgian governments in advance of the decision to close Vilvoorde. He said it was a few days before the official announcement.
However the newspaper Le Monde said Juppe's office had known about the Renault plan since mid-January.
Borotra told Europe 1 radio that Schweitzer had come to see him a few days before the Vilvoorde decision was announced.
"I told him -- you take your responsibility and as a shareholder I will judge your policy by its results," he said.
Asked if Dehaene, who has bitterly attacked the Renault move, was informed in advance, Borotra said: "Of course, in the days before the announcement."
His comment appeared to contradict a parliamentary answer he gave on Tuesday in which he said the French authorities had been neither informed nor consulted in advance.
Borotra said the decision to close Vilvoorde was necessary to reduce costs and respond to competition. "Restructurings cannot be avoided," he said, adding "even Renault can die".

The Belgian government dramatised its displeasure on Tuesday night by cancelling an order for 150 Renault cars. Interior Minister Johan Vande Lanotte announced the decision on RTBF radio after calls by Belgian tabloid newspapers for a boycott of Renault cars.
